summary: Extends the input of the get-bootstrapping-data call from RFC 8572 so a device can include a certificate signing request when it bootstraps. In reply, the device can receive an identity certificate, such as an IEEE 802.1AR Local Device Identifier, together with its onboarding information.

eli5.summary: When a new device first joins a network, it can now also ask for its own ID card in the same visit where it gets its starting instructions, instead of making a second trip.

questions: how to get a certificate during zero touch provisioning
what csr formats does sztp support
subtitle: How a new network device asks for its own identity certificate while it is first being set up.

tldr.problem: A device bootstrapping with SZTP (RFC 8572) normally relies on an identity certificate from its manufacturer. A certificate built for the real production environment would be better, but SZTP had no way to ask for one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9646 adds optional certificate signing request (CSR) support to the get-bootstrapping-data RPC. The device says what CSRs it can make, the server asks for one, the device sends it, and the signed certificate comes back inside the onboarding information.
tldr.outcome: A device can obtain an identity certificate such as an IEEE 802.1AR LDevID during bootstrapping, without relying on the manufacturer CA. It cannot be used with an untrusted bootstrap server.

today: RFC 9646 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8572. The listed metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Getting an Identity During Bootstrapping
sections.content:
RFC 9646 extends the input of the get-bootstrapping-data RPC from RFC 8572 (Secure Zero Touch Provisioning, SZTP) with an optional certificate signing request (CSR). The device can then also receive an identity certificate, for example a Local Device Identifier (LDevID) from IEEE 802.1AR, as part of the onboarding information in the reply.

A certificate made for the production environment removes the reliance on the manufacturer Certification Authority (CA). It also lets the device join production with an appropriate identity and other attributes in its certificate.

The document uses the terms SZTP-client (a device using a bootstrap server as a source of bootstrapping data) and SZTP-server (another name for the bootstrap server). Two YANG modules are defined: ietf-ztp-types and ietf-sztp-csr.
sections.eli5: A new gadget usually carries an ID card from the factory. This lets it also get a new ID card made for the place where it will actually work.

sections.title: The Four-Step Exchange
sections.content:
The exchange runs in the order of intended use:

  • The client sends a csr-support node in a first get-bootstrapping-data request. It says whether the client can generate a new asymmetric key, which key algorithms it supports, and which kinds of CSR it can generate.
  • The server answers with an error containing a csr-request structure. This selects the key algorithm, the CSR format, and optionally the content of the CSR itself.
  • The client sends one of the *-csr nodes in a second request.
  • The server replies with onboarding information that carries the signed certificate.

In the RFC's example the server's request for a CSR is an HTTP 400 Bad Request with the error tag missing-attribute. The server is expected to validate the CSR's origin and proof-of-possession, perhaps with a backend CA or registration authority (RA), before issuing the certificate.
sections.eli5: The gadget says "I can make an ID request". The server says "please make one like this". The gadget sends it, and the server mails back the finished ID card.

sections.title: The Two YANG Modules
sections.content:
The ietf-ztp-types module defines three groupings, one for each message between client and server: csr-support-grouping, csr-request-grouping and csr-grouping. It is kept separate so that bootstrapping protocols other than SZTP can reuse them.

The ietf-sztp-csr module augments the SZTP RPC input with the csr-support and csr nodes, and defines the csr-request structure that travels in the error-info node of a RESTCONF error.

Three CSR formats are supported: p10-csr (a PKCS #10 CertificationRequest from RFC 2986), cmc-csr (a profiled Full PKI Request from RFC 5272) and cmp-csr (a profiled PKIMessage from RFC 4210). If the server supplies cert-req-info, the client MUST use that structure to build its CSR.
sections.eli5: The modules are like blank forms. One form says what you can do, one says what is wanted, and one holds the actual request.

sections.title: Delivering the Certificate
sections.content:
How the signed certificate is carried inside the onboarding information is outside the scope of the document. Some implementations might use a script such as the pre-configuration-script, while others use the SZTP configuration node. The examples assume the client understands the ietf-keystore module from RFC 9642.

Two cases are shown. In the first, the certificate is for the same key as the manufacturer-generated certificate (an IDevID), so the new LDevID is attached to the existing key. In the second, the certificate is for a newly generated key, so a new key entry is added.

The device often needs the issuer's signing certificate too, so it can authenticate peers signed by the same issuer. One way to configure it is the ietf-truststore module from RFC 9641.
sections.eli5: The new ID card can be stapled to the old key the gadget already has, or to a brand new key it just made.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of RFC 8572 apply. For the client, the private key behind the new certificate MUST be protected from disclosure. It is RECOMMENDED that devices have a hardware security module such as a TPM. Without one, the key and certificate should be reset periodically. It is RECOMMENDED to generate a new private key for each CSR.

The solution cannot be used with an untrusted SZTP-server, because the HTTP error message cannot be signed data. Clients SHOULD NOT send csr-support to an untrusted server and SHOULD pass signed-data-preferred instead.

A raw PKCS #10 CSR does not support origin authentication, while CMP and CMC do, using either PKI or a shared secret. If a client must choose, it is RECOMMENDED to use the asymmetric key. The server verifies proof-of-possession from the signature over the CSR and, when the manufacturer key is reused, proof-of-origin by validating the IDevID certification path.

The LDevID and a newly generated private key are considered user data and SHOULD be cleared when the device is reset to factory default.
sections.eli5: The secret key is like a house key, so it must be kept safe. And you should not hand in your ID request to a stranger you cannot check.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered two namespace URIs in the IETF XML Registry, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-sztp-csr and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ztp-types. It also registered the two YANG modules, ietf-sztp-csr and ietf-ztp-types, in the YANG Module Names registry, both referencing RFC 9646.
sections.eli5: The two new forms were written into an official list so nobody else uses the same names.
